subject: Copywriting
title: The First Newspaper Ad
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The First Newspaper Ad.

hook.text: In 1704, the Boston News-Letter ran America's first newspaper ad. It offered a Long Island estate for sale.

buildup.text: Early newspaper ads were plain text, squeezed between news. No headlines, no images, no design at all.

discovery.text: Benjamin Franklin changed everything. He added white space and illustrations to ads in his Pennsylvania Gazette.

twist.text: Franklin wrote many ads himself. He understood that how an ad looked mattered as much as what it said.

climax.text: By 1800, ads funded most newspapers. Journalism depended on commerce from the start.

punchline.text: Newspapers didn't add ads. Ads created newspapers.

quiz.question: Who pioneered using white space and illustrations in newspaper ads?

details.summary: The first newspaper advertisement appeared in a 1625 English newsbook, promoting a book. As newspapers proliferated in the 17th and 18th centuries, advertising became their primary revenue model — a business arrangement that shaped media economics for four centuries and continues into the...
details.whyItMatters: The newspaper ad created the advertising-supported media model that funds journalism, social media, and search engines today. Understanding this origin explains modern media's dependence on advertising revenue.
takeaways: The first newspaper ad appeared in England in 1625
Advertising revenue became newspapers' primary business model
This ad-supported media model persists in digital platforms today

faq.question: How did advertising become central to newspaper economics?
faq.answer: Publishers discovered that ad revenue allowed them to sell papers below production cost, increasing circulation, which attracted more advertisers. This virtuous cycle made advertising-supported media the dominant model — the same economics that drive free social media platforms.

faq.question: What did early newspaper ads look like?
faq.answer: Early newspaper ads were simple classified-style text notices — no images, no headlines, just factual descriptions of goods and services. Display advertising with illustrations, borders, and large headlines didn't emerge until the 19th century.
